title: McLintock!

evidence.note: Wikipedia says Batjac failed to renew the copyright, that the copyright expired in 1991, and that the film was released by United Artists on November 13, 1963. Wikipedia also says a 1994 legal case determined the film was in the US public domain. It cites a Billboard headline from May 14, 1994 ('Court Rules for GoodTimes in McLintock! Case'). It also lists later litigation: Maljack Productions v. UAV Corp. (1997), consolidated with Batjac Productions, Inc. v. GoodTimes Home Video Corp., decided by the Ninth Circuit on Nov. 5, 1998 (48 U.S.P.Q.2d 1647). No Catalog of Copyright Entries volume (for example Motion Pictures 1991) and no Copyright Office public-records search was run for this dossier, so there is no CCE-level primary-source result and the print is not marked verified.

A stronger, directly on-point primary source than Wikipedia exists in this same litigation family. The related, consolidated Ninth Circuit opinion Maljack Productions, Inc. v. GoodTimes Home Video Corp., 81 F.3d 881 (9th Cir. 1996) — fetched directly — states as a holding: 'The McLintock motion picture copyright expired in 1991, and the film itself is public domain work.' Batjac Productions, Inc. v. GoodTimes Home Video Corp., 160 F.3d 1223 (9th Cir. 1998) (docket 97-55947, decided 1998-11-05) is the later appeal in the same McLintock! copyright dispute that Wikipedia's article on this film also names; its full text could not be fetched directly in this pass (court-opinion hosts returned access errors), so it is cited by name and docket rather than quoted. A federal appellate holding directly on this film's copyright status is stronger evidence than a secondary summary of it either way.
evidence.source: Maljack Productions, Inc. v. GoodTimes Home Video Corp., 81 F.3d 881 (9th Cir. 1996)

evidence.note: The film's theme was renewed as a separate musical work: RE0000531720 (1991), 'McLintock's theme. From McLintock.', claimant EMI Catalogue Partnership. So at least the theme music is protected even if the film print is free; check every cue before reusing the soundtrack.
evidence.source: U.S. Copyright Office Public Records System, RE0000531720

evidence.note: Frank De Vol score plus the song 'Love in the Country'; separate registration status not verified here.

Wikipedia credits the screenplay to James Edward Grant and says the film is loosely based on Shakespeare's The Taming of the Shrew. The Shakespeare source is free. The screenplay itself is original and is tied to the film's own copyright, whose renewal record I did not verify from primary sources.

No trademark search was done, and no right-of-publicity research was done. These are separate issues. Trademark covers the title or other marks used in commerce. The right of publicity is a state-law right over a person's name and likeness, and it can be held by an estate or licensing company. Either can outlast copyright expiry. Neither was searched, so both are undetermined.

A faithful restoration of a public-domain film adds no new US copyright: copying or restoring public-domain images without original creative additions is not protected (Bridgeman Art Library v. Corel Corp., S.D.N.Y. 1999, following Feist v. Rural, 1991). What a restoration ADDS can be protected: a newly composed or newly recorded score, colorization, newly written or translated titles and subtitles, and other original additions. Separately, ripping a copy-protected Blu-ray or DVD can break the DMCA's anti-circumvention rule (17 U.S.C. 1201) even when the film itself is public domain.
evidence.source: Bridgeman Art Library v. Corel Corp. (summary)

evidence.note: 17 U.S.C. 1201 - circumvention of copyright protection systems.
Paramount's restored HD releases carry new protectable elements; archival prints are the free source.

watch.quality: Unverified community upload (Oct 29, 2026). The uploader describes it as a 4K scan of the original camera negative and applied a Public Domain Mark themselves. The main file name (2160p ... WEB-DL ... SMURF.mkv) suggests a rip of a commercial streaming release, not an archival source. It may be a restored edition or an upscale with its own rights, and its provenance and rights are not confirmed.

editorial:
McLintock! is a 1963 comedy western directed by Andrew V. McLaglen and written by James Edward Grant. United Artists released it on November 13, 1963, and it loosely adapts Shakespeare's The Taming of the Shrew. According to Wikipedia, Batjac failed to renew the copyright, and the copyright expired in 1991. Wikipedia also reports a 1994 legal case and later Ninth Circuit litigation (Batjac Productions v. GoodTimes Home Video, 1998). We did not read those opinions or check their later history, and they should not be treated as settling anything. We also ran no Catalog of Copyright Entries or Copyright Office search, so the print layer stays undetermined here.

The music is the open question. Wikipedia says the score stayed under copyright and that Batjac retains the score rights. We could not verify any renewal record for the score or theme, so the score layer is undetermined. A creator who wants the footage should check or replace the soundtrack. Remastered releases exist (Paramount 2005 DVD, Olive Films 2013 Blu-ray, Paramount 2014 Blu-ray), and an edition may add protected material of its own. We did not research what those editions add.
faq: Wikipedia says the copyright was not renewed and expired in 1991, and it reports a 1994 legal case on the question. We checked no renewal records and did not read the court opinions or their later history. Treat the print as unconfirmed and verify it before commercial use.
Can I reuse the music from McLintock!?

Not safely. Wikipedia says the score remained under copyright. We could not verify the renewal details for the score or theme, so check the full music cue sheet and the renewal records, or replace the audio.
